input:
In this example, we consider a flat wall made of firebrick that has a thickness of 20 mm and separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the firebrick wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and careful measurement shows that the temperature difference across the wall is 276 K. When steady, one-dimensional conduction through the wall is assumed, the resulting heat flux works out to 15180 W m-2, which is a strikingly large value.

It is worth walking through how this number is obtained. The heat flux can be calculated by taking the thermal conductivity, multiplying it by the temperature difference, and dividing it by the wall thickness, which gives 1.1 × 276 / 0.02 = 15180 W m-2 once the thickness is expressed as 0.02 m. In other words, the whole result is determined by just four quantities, and nothing else about the two streams needs to be known. Because heat flux means the heat transferred per unit area per unit time, the large figure essentially reflects the combination of a large temperature difference and a thin wall, even though firebrick itself is a poor conductor of heat.

It should be noted, however, that surface (film) resistances have been left out of this estimate. If they were included, they would add resistance in series with the wall, and the actual flux would come out lower than 15180 W m-2. The quoted figure is therefore best understood as the wall-only value, and anyone wanting a design figure for the streams would need the film resistances as well.
target:
A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 276 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through the wall gives a heat flux of 15180 W m-2.

The flux follows from the conductivity, the temperature difference and the thickness in one step: 1.1 × 276 / 0.02 = 15180 W m-2, with the thickness taken as 0.02 m. Four quantities fix the result, and no other property of the streams enters it. The wall temperature field is taken as settled, and the same flux passes every plane parallel to the faces. Heat flux is the heat transferred per unit area of wall per unit time, stated here in watts per square metre. The figure is large because the temperature difference is large and the wall is thin; the conductivity of firebrick is low, and the thinness and the temperature difference outweigh it in the product.

Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate. Including them adds resistance in series with the wall and lowers the flux below 15180 W m-2; the figure is therefore the wall-only value, and a design figure for the streams requires the film resistances that this estimate omits. Used as it stands, the estimate bounds the duty from above.
